value.overview: The Red-crowned Woodpecker (Melanerpes rubricapillus) is a medium-sized tropical woodpecker of Central and northern South America. It is named for the red crown and nape of the male, while females usually show a duller crown and reddish nape. The species often lives in open, partly wooded landscapes as well as forests, and it readily uses gardens, plantations, mangroves, and forest edges. Its bold black-and-white pattern and pale underparts make it conspicuous while feeding or calling.
value.classification: The Red-crowned Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Melanerpes. It is closely related to several other Melanerpes woodpeckers, including Hoffmann’s Woodpecker, with which it can hybridize in parts of Costa Rica.
value.identification: About 20–21 cm long, this woodpecker has a barred black-and-white back and wings, a white rump, dark wings and tail, and pale buff or grayish underparts. Adult males have red on the crown and nape. Females generally have a buff or gray crown with less extensive red on the nape. In southwestern Costa Rica, especially near the Tárcoles region, individuals may show intermediate or orange nape coloration because of hybridization with Hoffmann’s Woodpecker. The species has a stout bill and a distinctive undulating flight.
value.rangeHabitat: The Red-crowned Woodpecker ranges from southwestern Costa Rica through Panama and into northern and central Colombia, northern Venezuela, the Guianas, and Tobago, with additional populations on some nearby islands. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the southern Pacific slope, occurring commonly from the Tárcoles area southward, including parts of Puntarenas and the Osa and Golfo Dulce regions; it also reaches inland sites such as San Isidro de El General. It uses mature and secondary forest, clearings, woodland edges, scrub, mangroves, plantations, pastures with trees, and gardens, mostly from sea level to about 1,700 m.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally resident throughout its range. It does not undertake regular long-distance seasonal migration, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The species nests in cavities excavated in dead or partly dead trees, branches, palms, or similar woody structures. Pairs may also use existing cavities. Breeding dates vary across its range; in Costa Rica and Panama, nesting activity is reported mainly from about February through July. The female usually lays a small clutch of white eggs, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the nestlings. Suitable dead wood and mature trees are important for providing nesting sites.
value.dietFeeding: Red-crowned Woodpeckers eat a mixture of fruit, berries, seeds, and animal prey. Fruit can form a large part of the diet, including cultivated papayas, bananas, and other garden or plantation crops. They also take insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates from bark, foliage, dead wood, and the ground. They forage by clinging to trunks and branches, probing or pecking into substrates, and occasionally catching prey in short flights.
value.behavior: This is an active, conspicuous woodpecker that commonly calls and drums from exposed branches, snags, and tall trees. It forages at several levels, from the ground and understory to the canopy, and often visits open habitats and human-altered areas. Individuals may occur singly, in pairs, or in small family groups. Like other woodpeckers, it uses drumming and vocal calls to defend territory and maintain contact, and it may roost in tree cavities.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely quantified, but it is not currently considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category.
